# Do carrots improve night vision?

**Verdict:** 📚 Published evidence only

## What the research and analysis found

The published evidence does not give a clear yes or no for whether daily carrots improve night vision in people with normal vision. Some studies suggest carrots can help restore normal dark adaptation in people with low vitamin A or night blindness, but not improve vision beyond normal levels. [sc11dc2d3-effect, s991b1102-effect, s685d0e97-effect, sff0d1a1e-effect] Other evidence points the other way: one study found increased carrot consumption was associated with more reported poor night vision among women. [s3c555109-effect] Because the best studies point in different directions and much of the evidence is about different populations or exposures, certainty is low.

## Question (PECO)

- **Population:** adults and children with normal vision
- **Exposure:** daily consumption of carrots, typically 1 medium-sized raw or cooked carrot
- **Comparator:** no carrot consumption
- **Outcome:** ability to see in low-light conditions, measured using standardized visual acuity tests in dim lighting (e.g., visual field tests under 10 lux)
- **Time window:** after 4 weeks of regular carrot consumption
- **Estimand:** ATE, mean difference, deviations handled as received

## Causal graph (DAG)

- carrot_consumption → night_vision_acuity: the question being tested
- carrot_consumption → vitamin_a_status: cites s6d91957d-effect, s15c3d923-effect, sadd25cc3-effect
- vitamin_a_status → night_vision_acuity: cites sff0d1a1e-effect, sadd25cc3-effect
- age → night_vision_acuity: assumed (no source)
- age → carrot_consumption: assumed (no source)
- diet_quality → carrot_consumption: assumed (no source)
- diet_quality → night_vision_acuity: assumed (no source)
- vitamin_a_supplementation → vitamin_a_status: cites sc11dc2d3-effect
- macular_pigment_optical_density → night_vision_acuity: cites s674eb79f-effect, sbba531d4-effect
- carotenoid_intake → macular_pigment_optical_density: cites s674eb79f-effect
- carrot_consumption → carotenoid_intake: assumed (no source)

Treated as exogenous (the model's judgment that nothing in the graph can cause it; no source): age, diet_quality, vitamin_a_supplementation.

## Key confounders

- age
- diet_quality

## Evidence

**Certainty:** low (starts high: a trial or a review of trials matches; down one: best studies point in different directions (+, -); down one: best evidence is about a different population or exposure)

Evidence flow: 140 sources found → 122 studies after dedupe → 23 included (excluded: not_a_study 11, wrong_population 5, off_topic 51, wrong_exposure 14, wrong_outcome 18).

- [Randomized control study on the effects of cooked carrots on night blindness in pregnant women](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/fact-or-fiction-carrots-improve-your-vision) — RCT, 2005, known only from secondary sources: a regular diet of the cooked carrots for six weeks helped to bring women’s response to darkness to normal levels
- [Night Vision and Carotenoids (NVC): A Randomized Placebo Controlled Clinical Trial on Effects of Carotenoid Supplementation on Night Vision in Older Adults.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8471486) — RCT, 2021: improvement in imputed composite crash risk score from a mean (SE) of 1.96 (0.19) to 1.29 (0.11) in the supplemented group (t-test p = 0.004)
- [Macular Pigment Optical Density as a Measurable Modifiable Clinical Biomarker.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11478551) — RCT, 2024: over a six-month period, participants who took a 14 mg Z + 7 mg L supplement experienced significant improvements in MPOD, glare recovery, contrast sensitivity, and preferred luminance
- [Comment on Richer et al. Night Vision and Carotenoids (NVC): A Randomized Placebo Controlled Clinical Trial on Effects of Carotenoid Supplementation on Night Vision in Older Adults. <i>Nutrients</i> 2021, <i>13</i>, 3191.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35807949) — RCT, 2022: effect not verified
- [Carrots, carotene and seeing in the dark.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10484191) — cross_sectional, 1999: Increased consumption of carrots, but no other food high in beta-carotene, was associated with significant increased reporting of poor night vision among women (P for trend = 0.04)
- [Dietary carotenoids and risk of age-related macular degeneration: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies](https://ubiehealth.com/doctors-note/recommends-nutrition-carotene-vision-detox-beta-4752q1) — systematic_review, 2014: effect not verified
- [A Systematic Review of Carotenoids in the Management of Age-Related Macular Degeneration.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3921/10/8/1255) — systematic_review, 2021: carotenoid supplementation resulted in significant improvements in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) and contrast sensitivity (CS) at all spatial frequencies in a dose-response relationship
- [Avocado consumption enhances human postprandial provitamin A absorption and conversion from a novel high-β-carotene tomato sauce and from carrots.](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4093981) — cross_sectional, 2014: The range of total carotene (i.e., β-carotene + α-carotene) conversion to vitamin A from the carrot meal alone was 0–64%, with a mean of 27%, and the carrot with avocado meal was 8–69%, with a mean of 34%
- [Spinach or carrots can supply significant amounts of vitamin A as assessed by feeding with intrinsically deuterated vegetables.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16210712) — cross_sectional, 2005: spinach tbeta-carotene conversion to retinol was 20.9 ± 9.0 to 1 (range: 10.0-46.5 to 1) and carrot tbeta-carotene conversion to retinol was 14.8 ± 6.5 to 1 (range: 7.7-24.5 to 1) by weight
- [Do Carrots help improve Night Vision?](https://www.westsideeyeclinic.com.au/carrots-vitamin-a-night-vision) — other, year unknown, known only from secondary sources: eating carrots could help to correct and improve your night vision, but only to match the capabilities of an average person in ordinary health – it won’t give you the ability to see in complete darkness or at a higher than average level
- [Myth or Fact: Eating Carrots Improves Eyesight](https://www.dukehealth.org/blog/myth-or-fact-eating-carrots-improves-eyesight) — other, 2013, known only from secondary sources: effect not verified
- [Age-Related Eye Diseases Studies (AREDS & AREDS 2)](https://www.nvisioncenters.com/diet-and-eye-health/beta-carotene) — other, year unknown, known only from secondary sources: a combination of vitamins and other micronutrients can reduce the risk of age-macular degeneration (AMD) by up to 25 percent
- [Mechanisms of vitamin A metabolism and deficiency in the mammalian and fly visual system.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8172435) — other, 2021: effect not verified
- [Relative contribution of α-carotene to postprandial vitamin A concentrations in healthy humans after carrot consumption.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5486200) — other, 2017: α-carotene contributed 12–35% of newly converted vitamin A (predicted contribution = 25.5%)
- [The effect of food preparation on the bioavailability of carotenoids from carrots using intrinsic labelling.](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effect-of-food-preparation-on-the-bioavailability-of-carotenoids-from-carrots-using-intrinsic-labelling/C4E2B9F580B2F6D142A7E48DC52953D9) — other, 2012: effect not verified
- [The Rod Photoreceptor Cell](https://kindsight.com.au/news/eye-health/carrot-vision-myth) — other, year unknown, known only from secondary sources: eating more carrots really could help [with night vision] if deficient in Vitamin A, but once the body has enough beta-carotene, further consumption won’t improve night vision
- [Carrots Can't Help You See in the Dark. Here's How a World War II Propaganda Campaign Popularized the Myth](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/carrots-cant-help-you-see-in-the-dark-heres-how-world-war-ii-propaganda-campaign-popularized-the-myth-28812484) — other, 2013, known only from secondary sources: eating carrots does not improve night vision in people who are healthy
- [The eye signs of vitamin A deficiency.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3936686) — other, 2013: effect not verified
- [Do Carrots Actually Improve Eyesight?](https://gaileyeyeclinic.com/carrots-actually-improve-eyesight) — other, 2009, known only from secondary sources: Carrots contain beta-carotene, a substance that the body converts to vitamin A, an important nutrient for eye health. An extreme lack of vitamin A can cause blindness.
- [Are Carrots Good for Your Eyes?](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/are-carrots-good-for-your-eyes) — other, year unknown, known only from secondary sources: Carrots are especially high in the antioxidants lutein and beta-carotene, which have been shown to protect your eyes.
- [Carrots: Health Benefits, Nutrition Facts, and Risks](https://www.webmd.com/food-recipes/benefits-carrots) — other, year unknown, known only from secondary sources: Beta carotene in carrots helps keep your eyes healthy. It helps protect your eyes from the sun and lowers your chances of cataracts and other eye problems.
- [Nutrition and Health Benefits of Carrots](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/foods/carrots) — other, 2026, known only from secondary sources: Individuals with low vitamin A levels are more likely to experience night blindness, a condition that may diminish by eating carrots or other foods rich in vitamin A or carotenoids.
- [The Real Connection Between Carrots and Vision](https://www.mcgill.ca/oss/article/did-you-know-nutrition/real-connection-between-carrots-and-vision) — other, year unknown, known only from secondary sources: vision benefits will only be seen when there is a deficiency of vitamin A

## Estimate

No estimate was computed for this question.

## Limitations

- Certainty is low because the best studies point in different directions and the best evidence is about a different population or exposure.
- No usable dataset was found, so the answer relies on published claims rather than a direct analysis of data.
- Some supporting evidence comes from pregnant women with night blindness or older adults taking carotenoid supplements, not from healthy adults and children eating carrots. [sc11dc2d3-effect, sed456286-effect]
- One study found increased carrot consumption was associated with more reported poor night vision among women, which conflicts with the idea that carrots help. [s3c555109-effect]

## 🧞 Genie's aside

If carrots could turn us all into owls, the produce aisle would be a very different place at midnight. Read the studies listed above to see how the evidence lines up.
